Coyote Creek Channel passes along the western side of the Olinder are and is lined with a riparian woodland consisting of a combination of native and exotic (introduced) species. Exotics include Blue Gum and California Pepper while natives include Box Elder, Blue Elderberry, Live Oak, Willow and Sycamore. Growing beneath the canopy afforded by the trees, there is an understory of shrubs, vines and herbacious species. Many of these plants are an important food, source for wildlife along Coyote Creek as well as providing cover and nesting areas. Birdlife found along the Creek includes such species as Belted Kingfisher, Red-Shafted Flicker, Black Phoebe, Robin, BrownTowhee and Golden-Crowned Sparrow. Mammals of the Creek are: Audubon Cottontail, Fox Squirrel, Botta Pocket Gopher, and Oppossum. The herptiles expected are: Western Fence Lizard Lizzard and California Slender Salamander. This list is not meant to be exhaustive but rather typify some common species found along the Creek. Generally, in urbanized areas, riparian vegetation is the lost vestige of the former biotic community. The rich habitat found along the creek supports a number of wildlife species not found throughout the city. Further, this riparian habitat, to some extent, acts as a wildlife corridor through the urban area and serves as a visual cue for birds. Some of the creekside wildlife species like Fox, Squirrels, Western Fences Lizard Golden-Crowned Sparrows, Brown Towhee and Robins can be found elsewhere across the project area.
E. TRANSPORTATION AND TRAFFIC
The private passenger automobile and public transit are the dominant travel modes in San Jose, with movement via private auto dwarfing the utilization of public transit. With the exception of the Southern Pacific Company's passenger rail link extending from San Jose to San Francisco, both modes of transit use an extensive road network. The street network within San Jose includes approximately 1,412 miles of street owned and maintained by the City of San Jose, the County of Santa Clara and the State of California. It is estimated that in 1975 the Citywide road net (freeway, expressway, arterial, collector), considered as a functional transportation unit, will carry approximately 2.1 million person trips daily (Santa Clara Valley Water District, 1974).
Highways 17, 161, and 280 form the framework into which the lower capacity roads feed. The absence of a comprehensive circulation pattern is related to the low density pattern of residential development prevalent throughout much of San Jose. The general outline of traffic distribution in these thoroughfares is one in which traffic volumes (both average daily trip numbers ADT) and peak-hour trips) increase rapidly as central San Jose is approached. Highway 101 is the main north/south freeway spine linking San Jose with the urban centers of Northern Santa Clara County and the San Francisco Penninsula. Portions of this freeway between I-280 and the San Tomas Expressway are operating near design capacity during peak-hour operations and the two-land (each direction) segment opposite downtown San Jose is above capacity during similar periods.
